title: Refactoring, Debugging, Code Review & Think-Aloud
description: Turing Stage 3 alternative format: refactor/debug a dirty 500-line codebase in 35 min. Andela pair-programming narration + SOLID refactor. Now includes PR review drills (Andela's most common pair-round pattern). Each drill is open-rubric — pull the linked snippet locally, work aloud, then self-score.

12.4 Code Review Drills: Read for correctness → security → readability → tests
Approve with note vs request changes

questions.prompt: Rehearsal drill: describe how you'd approach a live coding round for the first 3 minutes BEFORE writing any code. Say it aloud.

rubric.criterion: Restate the problem in your own words
Ask 2-3 clarifying questions about input shape, constraints, edge cases
State assumptions explicitly
Sketch approach + BigO + trade-offs before typing
Confirm the plan with the interviewer before coding

questions.modelAnswer: Say: 'Let me repeat back — I need to X given Y with constraints Z. A few clarifications: (1) is input always sorted? (2) any duplicates? (3) what's N? Assuming N up to 1M and unsorted with duplicates, my first approach would be a hash-map based two-pass solution: O(n) time, O(n) space. There's a two-pointer solution that's O(1) extra space but O(n log n) if we can sort. Given the constraints, hash-map is simpler — should I go with that or would you prefer the space-optimal version?'

rubric.criterion: Names each responsibility: input parsing, validation, persistence, side-effects (email, event), audit
Proposes layered structure: controller (thin) → service (business logic) → repository (DB) → notifier/publisher
Domain logic (validation, price/balance math) lives in a pure/testable function without I/O
Uses dependency injection for external services (SES, Kafka) so unit tests can mock them
Handles transaction boundary + outbox pattern for the email + Kafka publish
Doesn't over-engineer — pragmatic split, not 20 files for a small handler

questions.modelAnswer: Split into: 1) OrderController (thin, HTTP → DTO → calls service). 2) OrderService (business logic, orchestrates repo + events, pure where possible). 3) OrderRepository (DB reads/writes). 4) InventoryService (side-effectful DB dec). 5) NotificationOutbox (write to outbox table in same txn; separate worker sends email + Kafka). 6) AuditLogger (interface, injected). Tests: unit-test OrderService with mocks; integration-test with real DB + testcontainers. Controller shrinks to ~10 lines.

questions.prompt: A test fails intermittently in CI (~1 in 20 runs) but always passes locally. Walk through your debug approach.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't 'just add a retry' as the first move
Considers common causes: shared mutable state between tests, timing/race, non-deterministic order, external I/O, clock
Reproduces via loop + parallelism + CI-like environment
Isolates by running the flaky test in different orderings / alone
Fixes root cause (not the symptom); adds regression assertion

questions.modelAnswer: Reproduce first: `for i in {1..100}; do npm test -- --testNamePattern='X' || break; done`, then with `--runInBand` vs parallel. Common culprits: (a) tests share global state (module-level cache, DB row not cleaned), (b) timezone/locale between local and CI, (c) time-based assertion (`Date.now()`), (d) network to real service (should be mocked), (e) filesystem race (parallel tests using same tmp dir). Fix the underlying nondeterminism; add a comment tying it to the incident.

questions.prompt: An API endpoint that was P95 = 80ms now takes 800ms after last week's deploy. No error rate change. Diagnose in 15 minutes.

rubric.criterion: Diff the deploy first (commits since last known good, config, feature flags)
Trace one slow request end-to-end (distributed trace or request log with span timings)
Consider N+1 introduced by an ORM include change or missing index
Check external dependency: cache eviction rate, upstream latency, retry storm
Considers cold-cache after deploy vs warm baseline

questions.modelAnswer: Step 1: git log since deploy. Step 2: open a slow trace — where is the 720ms spent? DB, external HTTP, in-process? Step 3: if DB, EXPLAIN a slow query; check if a new .include('...') added an N+1 or a new column with no index. Step 4: if cache — is hit rate down? An eviction change or key change? Step 5: if external HTTP — retry policy change, timeout change, downstream latency spike? Rollback candidate identified within the window if root cause matches deploy diff.

questions.prompt: You inherit a 400-line React component. What's your refactor sequence?

rubric.criterion: Don't refactor blindly — first read/write tests to lock behavior
Extract data-fetching into a custom hook (useX)
Extract form state / validation into another hook or a reducer
Split render into subcomponents by section, each with its own props
Memoize expensive derivations only after measuring
Commit in small reviewable chunks (avoid one giant PR)

questions.modelAnswer: Order: (1) capture behavior in tests (React Testing Library — user-facing assertions), (2) pull data-fetching + caching into useX hook, (3) pull form state / mutations into useReducer or react-hook-form, (4) split the JSX into subcomponents by visual section, (5) profile with React DevTools before adding memoization, (6) each step = its own commit + PR-sized chunk. Behavior unchanged; complexity local.

questions.prompt: Node.js API OOMs (out of memory) after ~48h of steady traffic. Debug approach.

rubric.criterion: Distinguishes memory-leak (grows unbounded) vs high-baseline (fits but tight)
Takes heap snapshots at intervals with --inspect / clinic.js / heapdump
Compares snapshots to find retained-size growth by object type
Common suspects: closures capturing large scope, growing Map/Array without eviction, event listeners never removed, per-request cache keyed by user
Fix + verify by running load test with leak reproduction pre-fix

questions.modelAnswer: Enable --inspect. Take heap snapshot at hour 1, 6, 24. Diff. Look for objects with growing retained size. Common: a module-level Map used as a cache without eviction; event listeners added per request but not removed; setInterval closures keeping references. Fix, deploy with a canary, monitor RSS/heapUsed for 24h before full rollout.

questions.prompt: A junior submits a PR adding a global `axios.defaults.timeout = 60000` and a new retry wrapper `async function retry(fn) { for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) try { return await fn(); } catch {} }`. Give the review.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't just say 'no' — explains WHY
Global mutation is a footgun; scope timeout per request or per client instance
Silent catch swallows real bugs; must at least log + re-throw on final attempt
No backoff → retry storm on upstream failure
Retrying non-idempotent operations (POST) causes duplicates
Positive framing / suggests concrete fix

questions.modelAnswer: Comments: (1) mutating axios global affects every other caller — instantiate a scoped axios client instead. (2) the empty catch will hide real bugs and mask the last-attempt failure — at minimum, log with attempt number and rethrow after the loop. (3) no backoff → thundering herd on transient failures; add exp backoff + jitter. (4) applying retry to POST without idempotency key can create duplicates — either restrict retry to safe methods or require an idempotency key. Suggested rewrite with these fixes included so it's constructive.

questions.prompt: You must add a new feature to a 3000-line file with no tests, and you have 2 weeks. How do you proceed?

rubric.criterion: Doesn't propose a rewrite up front — that's 6 months of yak-shaving
Adds characterization tests around the affected paths BEFORE touching code
Uses the 'seam' pattern (Michael Feathers) — introduce dependency injection at the change point
Applies strangler-fig for new code: new feature in a small isolated module, called from the legacy file
Ships in small PRs; each one green in CI; doesn't block on giant refactor

questions.modelAnswer: Read the file top-to-bottom, take notes on responsibilities. Write characterization tests (assert current behavior, warts and all) around the two functions the feature touches. Introduce a seam — pass in the new dependency as a parameter. Build the new module in isolation, unit-test it fully, wire it in behind a feature flag. Ship. Cleanup can come later.

questions.prompt: A production incident just fired: 500 error rate spiked to 30% two minutes ago. First 10 minutes of your response.

rubric.criterion: Acknowledge the alert, join the incident channel
Check deploy timeline — was anything shipped in the last hour?
Check dashboards: which endpoint, which error, upstream health, DB health
Rollback OR feature-flag disable is the fastest recovery — don't try to fix forward under pressure
Communicate to stakeholders (status page, exec channel) with what you know + ETA

questions.modelAnswer: Ack alert, jump in call, page anyone missing. Ask: what changed in last hour? Look at first 5xx sample — same endpoint? Same error message? Upstream dep down? If a deploy happened, rollback FIRST, investigate SECOND. If a feature flag can turn off the broken path, flip it. Post status update: 'Investigating elevated 5xx errors; rolled back deploy X; will update in 10 min.' Stay in the channel.

questions.prompt: A function is called 10k times per request and profiles to 40% of request CPU. It's 30 lines of pure logic. How do you approach optimization?

rubric.criterion: Measure with a real profile — don't guess
Ask if we can call it fewer times first (memoize / hoist / batch)
Look for accidental O(n²) / allocations inside a hot loop
Consider caching / precomputation if inputs repeat
Only reach for lower-level optimizations after algorithmic + call-graph fixes
Add a benchmark to lock the improvement so it doesn't regress

questions.modelAnswer: Profile first — confirm 40%. Ask: can we call it 100 times instead of 10k (memoize, hoist out of the loop, batch)? If not, look for hidden quadratics — `Array.includes` inside a loop → convert to Set; string concatenation → array + join; JSON parse/stringify per call → pass parsed object. If still hot, cache by input hash. Add a benchmark to CI to prevent regression.

questions.prompt: Two users report seeing each other's data one time each. Debug approach.

rubric.criterion: Treats as a security incident — audit + freeze if scope is unclear
Common causes: shared module-level state on the server, cache key missing user_id, JWT/session confusion
Check for stateful things at module scope (variables outside handlers), especially after auth
Audit log query to find scope of the leak — how many users, which endpoints?
Fix + notify affected users + post-mortem

questions.modelAnswer: Treat as critical. Freeze deploys, page security. Common: (1) module-level cache keyed only on resource id, not user id — user A hits endpoint, user B's request lands on same node and gets A's cached data. (2) shared axios interceptor mutating req headers. (3) global user context leaking between requests (rare in Node's per-request model but possible with async_hooks misuse). Audit logs to bound the blast radius. Fix + write post-mortem + notify affected users per compliance.

questions.prompt: You just solved a LeetCode-medium in the interview. The interviewer says 'walk me through complexity and edge cases.' Do it now aloud for the 3Sum problem you solved.

rubric.criterion: States time complexity with derivation (sort O(n log n) + outer loop × two-pointer inner = O(n²))
States space complexity (O(1) extra, or O(n) if considering sort in JS)
Enumerates edge cases: empty, one, two elements, all same value, no triplet sums to 0, all negatives, duplicates
Names one improvement you'd make with more time (early termination, dedup on i-index)
Confident but honest — acknowledges limits

questions.modelAnswer: Time: O(n²) — sort is O(n log n), then for each of n elements a two-pointer inner scan is O(n). Space: O(1) extra, ignoring the output. Edge cases: empty and length<3 return []; all zeros should return one triplet; duplicates require skipping same values at i, l, and r positions after finding a triplet; all negatives (or all positives) means we can early-terminate. If I had more time I'd add early termination when nums[i] > 0. One thing to watch: sort is destructive in JS if we don't want side effects — should confirm with the interviewer whether input can be mutated.

questions.prompt: Review this PR. A colleague submits: `async function saveUser(u) { try { await db.insert(u); } catch (e) { console.log(e); } }`. Give the review.

rubric.criterion: Names the silent swallow — errors get logged but the caller thinks it succeeded
Suggests rethrow or return a Result/Error type
console.log in prod path is wrong — use structured logger with level
No input validation of `u`
Constructive tone — 'suggest' not 'this is broken'

questions.modelAnswer: Two concrete asks: (1) swallowing the DB error means the caller can't recover — I'd rethrow after logging or return a discriminated Result. (2) `console.log` won't ship structured logs to our aggregator — use `logger.error({ userId: u.id, err }, 'saveUser failed')`. Also worth adding a zod schema on `u` at the boundary. Happy to pair on it if useful.

questions.prompt: PR adds `users.forEach(u => u.posts = await Post.find({ userId: u.id }))` inside a request handler serving 100 users at a time. Review.

rubric.criterion: Names the N+1 query pattern
Notes that `forEach` doesn't await — this is a race/wrong pattern too
Suggests: single query with WHERE userId IN (…) + group in memory, or ORM eager-load / include
Considers pagination — 100 users may not stay 100
Suggests DB index on Post.userId if missing

questions.modelAnswer: Two bugs stacked: (1) `forEach` doesn't await promises, so `u.posts` gets a pending Promise assigned and the handler races. (2) even if fixed with `for…of + await`, that's an N+1 — 1 query for users + 100 queries for posts. Better: `Post.find({ userId: { $in: users.map(u => u.id) } })` then group by userId in JS, or use the ORM's `include: [Post]`. Also worth checking the index on `Post.userId`.

questions.prompt: PR adds `app.get('/user/:id', (req, res) => db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`))`. Review.

rubric.criterion: Names SQL injection risk (raw interpolation)
Suggests parameterized query: `db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id])`
Notes SELECT * exposes all columns including password_hash — pick columns explicitly
Missing authz check — should the requester see this user?
No error handling / 404 for missing

questions.modelAnswer: Blockers: (1) SQL injection — must be parameterized; interpolation is CVE-territory. (2) `SELECT *` leaks columns like password_hash or PII — enumerate needed fields. (3) No authz — currently any logged-in user can pull any user's row; add ownership or role check. (4) No 404 handling. Suggested rewrite in the comment.

questions.prompt: PR adds a new function but the only test is `expect(add(2, 2)).toBe(4)`. Review.

rubric.criterion: Notes single happy-path test is insufficient
Asks for edge cases: negative, zero, floats, large numbers, non-numeric input
Asks about behavior on invalid input — throw? return NaN? Document
Suggests table-driven test / parameterized cases for readability
Coverage note — measure branches not just lines

questions.modelAnswer: One happy-path assertion isn't enough — I'd want: (a) at least one negative-input case, (b) zero, (c) float precision (0.1 + 0.2), (d) very large numbers approaching Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, (e) explicit case for what happens on non-numeric input (thrown TypeError? NaN? make it a documented contract with a test). Table-driven format keeps this readable. Andela weights test writing heavily on pair rounds.

questions.prompt: A colleague submits a 2000-line PR touching auth, database schema, and 3 unrelated bug fixes. How do you respond?

rubric.criterion: Doesn't just approve or dump 40 comments — asks to split the PR first
Names why: single-concern PRs are safer to revert, easier to review, easier to bisect regressions
Offers concrete split: (a) schema migration, (b) auth change, (c) each bug fix separately
Frames as help, not gatekeeping — 'happy to review each in <30 min'
Escalates only if the pattern repeats after conversation

questions.modelAnswer: First comment: 'This is a lot to review in one go — can we split into (a) schema migration + backfill, (b) the auth change, (c) each of the three bug fixes? Each of those has different rollback profiles, and if one needs to revert we don't lose the others. Happy to review each in under 30 min if we split it.' Don't approve, don't leave nitpicks yet — get the split first.

questions.prompt: Reviewer left 15 comments on your PR, several are opinion-based ('I'd prefer this style'). How do you respond?

rubric.criterion: Doesn't get defensive — treats review as help
Separates correctness/security fixes (accept) from style/opinion (discuss)
Asks 'why' on opinion items to learn or push back respectfully
For pure style, offers to add a linter rule to remove the class of debate
Merges what's clearly right + closes what's discussed with reasoning

questions.modelAnswer: Triage: (1) correctness/security → fix immediately, thank reviewer. (2) 'I'd prefer X' → reply 'what's the concern behind it?' — either learn something or explain my rationale for the current choice. (3) if it's genuinely just style, propose adding to lint config so the debate resolves once. Never merge silent — every comment gets an ack or a fix.

questions.prompt: Colleague submits a PR clearly generated by an AI assistant — works on happy path but adds try/catch swallowing everything, has invented API calls that don't exist, and duplicates a util you already have. Review.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't shame the tool — focuses on the code that shipped
Flags invented API calls (hallucinations) explicitly
Flags the swallowed try/catch
Points to the existing util that's being duplicated
Suggests: run it against real integration tests + grep for duplicates before opening

questions.modelAnswer: Two must-fixes: (1) `client.batchAsync()` on line 42 isn't a real method on our client — where did this come from? (2) the try/catch on line 60 swallows all errors including auth failures; needs to at least log and rethrow. Also: `lib/format.formatDate` already does exactly what your `dateFmt` function does — please use the existing one. For AI-assisted PRs, worth running against integration tests + a `git grep` for helpers before opening.
